title: Stage 5: Gateway route, autoscaling and the first upgrade
summary: Open the front door, scale with load, and ship 1.5 without dropping a request.

steps.title: The last pieces
body: parentRefs: [{ name: public, namespace: gateway }]   # the platform team's Gateway
scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: shop-api }
metrics: [{ type: Resource, resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } } }]
spec: { maxUnavailable: 1, selector: { matchLabels: { app: shop-api } } }
The Gateway `public` in namespace `gateway` belongs to the platform team: it holds the HTTPS listener and the `shop-tls` certificate. Your team only owns the route.
And on the Deployment: remove `replicas` (the HPA owns it) and set `strategy: { rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } }`.

steps.prompt: Release 1.5.0. Put the steps in order.
lines: Change the image tag in the Deployment manifest in Git and merge the PR
Argo CD (or kubectl apply) updates the Deployment
A new ReplicaSet starts one 1.5.0 pod (maxSurge 1)
The new pod passes its readiness probe and joins the Service
One 1.4.0 pod is removed; repeat until all pods run 1.5.0
steps.explain: If a 1.5.0 pod never becomes ready, the rollout stops at step 4 with every 1.4.0 pod still serving. Revert the commit to roll back.

steps.prompt: During the 1.5.0 rollout the HPA scales from 3 to 5. What does the Deployment controller do?
options: It keeps rolling: the new replica count applies, and the controller spreads the change across the old and new ReplicaSets
It scales only the old ReplicaSet
It ignores the HPA until the rollout finishes
steps.explain: Rollouts and scaling compose. That is why the Deployment must not also have `replicas` set in Git, or a sync would fight the HPA.

steps.title: Publish it with an HTTPRoute and ship v2 safely
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl`; the current namespace is `todo`, and the manifests live in `~/k8s`. The cluster has the Gateway API CRDs and the platform's Gateway `public` in `todo` (no gateway
controller runs here, so the route is validated and stored but nothing serves it).
1. Attach an `HTTPRoute` named `todo` to the Gateway `public` for the host `todo.example.com`, sending every path to
2. Ship v2 without ever dropping below 2 ready pods: set the rolling update to `maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`,
change the container's argument to `--name=todo-api-v2`, and wait for the rollout to complete.

checks.name: the route sends todo.example.com to todo-api:80
checks.cmd: kubectl get httproute todo -o json | jq -r '"\(.spec.parentRefs[0].name) \(.spec.hostnames[0]) \(.spec.rules[0].backendRefs[0].name):\(.spec.rules[0].backendRefs[0].port)"'
checks.fail: There should be an HTTPRoute `todo` on `public` for `todo.example.com` with the backend `todo-api:80`.

checks.name: v2 is fully rolled out
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/todo-api --timeout=40s >/dev/null; kubectl get deploy todo-api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].args} {.status.updatedReplicas} {.status.readyReplicas}'
checks.fail: All pods should run `--name=todo-api-v2`, 2 updated and ready.

hints: An HTTPRoute with `parentRefs: [{name: public}]`, `hostnames: [todo.example.com]` and one rule with `backendRefs: [{name: todo-api, port: 80}]` (no `matches` means every path).
Then change the args (`kubectl patch ... --type=json`, `replace` on `/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args`) and `kubectl rollout status deploy/todo-api`.
steps.explain: The app is now reachable the modern way: the platform's Gateway owns the listener, your HTTPRoute owns the host and the backend. And with `maxUnavailable: 0` plus a readiness probe, the release added one v2 pod at a time and removed a v1 pod only after its replacement was Ready, so capacity never dropped. If v2 had failed its probe, the rollout would have stalled with v1 still serving, and `kubectl rollout undo` would end it.

steps.title: Will it hold Black Friday?
prompt: Write `string Capacity(double peakRps, double rpsPerPodAt60Cpu, int maxReplicas, int nodeFreeCpuM, int podCpuRequestM)`:
- pods the cluster can fit = `nodeFreeCpuM / podCpuRequestM` (integer division)
- limit = the smaller of `maxReplicas` and what fits
- else if needed > `maxReplicas` and `maxReplicas` ≤ fits: `"raise maxReplicas to N"`
- else: `"add nodes: need N pods, room for F"`
starter: string Capacity(double peakRps, double rpsPerPodAt60Cpu, int maxReplicas, int nodeFreeCpuM, int podCpuRequestM)
solution: string Capacity(double peakRps, double rpsPerPodAt60Cpu, int maxReplicas, int nodeFreeCpuM, int podCpuRequestM)
if (needed > maxReplicas && maxReplicas <= fits) return $"raise maxReplicas to {needed}";
return $"add nodes: need {needed} pods, room for {fits}";
template: Dojo.Eq("HPA cap too low", "raise maxReplicas to 12", Capacity(1150, 100, 10, 8000, 250));
Dojo.Eq("cluster too small", "add nodes: need 12 pods, room for 8", Capacity(1150, 100, 20, 2000, 250));
hints: Compute the three numbers first, then the three outcomes in order.
steps.explain: This one stays a code step: it is capacity planning before the event, arithmetic over load-test numbers, with nothing in the cluster to look at yet.
